The patient presents with acute-onset sharp lower back pain and radicular leg pain extending laterally to the foot — a classic distribution for L5 or S1 nerve root involvement. The positive straight leg raise test (Measurement 9) strongly supports mechanical nerve root irritation, as this maneuver tensions the sciatic nerve and its proximal roots (L4–S1), particularly L5 and S1. - Positive straight leg raise test (Measurement 9) — sensitive indicator of lumbosacral nerve root irritation, especially L5/S1.  
- Absence of bowel or bladder dysfunction — excludes cauda equina syndrome, narrowing differential to non-emergent radiculopathy.  
- Intact sensation (light touch/pinprick) across L4–S1 dermatomes — indicates no sensory deficit, supporting early or inflammatory rather than severe compressive pathology.  
- No motor weakness on neurological exam — suggests no significant axonal compromise or chronic compression.  
- Normal patellar (L4) and Achilles (S1) reflexes — argues against substantial root-level disruption at those levels.  
- Lumbar spine MRI ordered specifically to evaluate for disc herniation — reflects clinical suspicion anchored in this diagnosis.

[GAPS]  
- MRI results are pending — definitive confirmation of disc herniation location, size, and degree of neural contact/compression is missing.  
- No documentation of Valsalva or cough exacerbation of pain — supportive but not essential feature of discogenic radiculopathy.  
- No assessment of paraspinal muscle spasm or tenderness — though not required for diagnosis, could support acute mechanical origin.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute lumbar disc herniation
